title: Production-bound compose set MSSQL_PID: Developer, which Microsoft licenses for development/test ONLY -- a licence violation once ACMP serves the real committee. FIXED IN BOTH HALVES, and the second half is the interesting one because the row sat Open while the first half was quietly done. (1) CLOUD, in slice P21: deploy/docker-compose.cloud.yml sets MSSQL_PID: Express, the free production licence. Express's limits are all satisfied there -- recordings live in S3 so the 10 GB/DB cap is ample for governance rows, jobs are Hangfire rather than SQL Agent, and the custom sqlserver-fts image installs Full-Text Search independent of edition (confirmed the hard way by DEF-018, which is an Express-specific AUTO_CLOSE defect and therefore itself proof that Express is the deployed edition). (2) ON-PREM PRODUCTION, found 2026-08-07 while reconciling this row against the code: deploy/docker-compose.prod.yml declares a sqlserver service block but NEVER overrode the base file's value, so `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.prod.yml` -- the composition that IS on-prem production -- still resolved to Developer and stayed in violation. The base file legitimately keeps Developer because that composition is the dev stack; the overlay is what turns it into production and is therefore where the edition belongs. Fixed by adding MSSQL_PID: Express to the overlay's sqlserver block (PR #186). VERIFIED BY RESOLVING BOTH COMPOSITIONS rather than by reading the file: base alone still renders MSSQL_PID: Developer (correct -- that is dev), and base plus the prod overlay renders MSSQL_PID: Express. The lesson worth keeping is the drift itself: this row read Open for the whole of PH-5 while the cloud half was shipped, so anyone reading the register would have believed the cloud environment was in violation when it was not, and would NOT have known the on-prem overlay actually was.

title: sqlserver-init.sh guarded the mandatory Keycloak RCSI setting with DATABASEPROPERTYEX('keycloak','IsReadCommittedSnapshotOn'), which is NOT a valid DATABASEPROPERTYEX property name and returns NULL. Since `NULL = 0` is never true, the guarded ALTER never fired and READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT was left OFF on the Keycloak database — the exact deadlock-prone configuration ADR-0036 exists to prevent. Caught by the U2 spike (RCSI read back NULL despite a healthy Keycloak). Fixed by reading the flag from sys.databases.is_read_committed_snapshot_on in both the guard and the verification echo; the U2 re-run then reported 'the fixed guard fired' and RCSI=1. The idempotency-under-live-connection pass before the fix was a false positive (the ALTER simply never ran).

title: The backup bind mount is unwritable by the process that writes backups. SQL Server writes the .bak itself, from inside its container, as uid 10001 (mssql) — not as the cron user running backup.sh. Docker creates a missing bind source ROOT-OWNED 0755, so every BACKUP DATABASE fails with 'Cannot open backup device ... Operating system error 5(Access is denied.)'. The failure mode is what makes it severe: it appears only in a 02:00 cron log, names an OS error rather than a permission model, and until someone reads that log the deployment looks backed up while never having written a single .bak. Latent in the P18b on-prem script too (it worked only because the directory happened to be created by hand). Caught by the P23 U4 restore drill BEFORE any cloud backup existed. Fixed in slice P23: backup.sh probes the mount from inside the container before it starts and refuses with the exact remediation (sudo install -d -o 10001 -g 10001 -m 0755 <dir>), and deploy/runbooks/cloud-backup-dr.md carries it as a one-time prerequisite.
custom_attributes: {"slice": "SL-023", "found_by": "P23 U4 drill (deploy/scripts/spike-cloud-gates.sh)", "location": "deploy/scripts/backup.sh"}

title: SQL Server EXPRESS forces AUTO_CLOSE ON for user databases, and an auto-closing database TEARS DOWN the full-text population — global search silently indexes nothing. This is an edition-change defect that arrives with PH-5: the on-prem Developer edition did not do it, Express does, and it is NOT inherited from `model` (verified live on the spike instance: model auto_close=0 while Acmp, keycloak and a scratch database were all 1). With AUTO_CLOSE ON the database shuts down whenever the last connection drops. The consequence is not merely a cold first query: it aborts the asynchronous full-text crawl. The U3 spike reproduced it end to end — an indexed Arabic row sat at populate-status 1 with 0 items indexed for over two minutes and CONTAINS returned 0 rows, because each poll connected, restarted the database, and killed the crawl it was measuring; the measurement was destroying what it measured. Setting AUTO_CLOSE OFF took the identical row through 1:0 → 1:1 → 4:1 → 0:1 and CONTAINS = 1 within about 15 seconds. Severity is driven by the failure MODE: nothing errors. Search returns zero results, the API logs are clean, the index exists, IsFullTextInstalled reports 1 and the word-breaker is present — every check we had said healthy while AC-060/AC-061 global search would have returned nothing in the cloud. It also masqueraded as flakiness for a full day (U3 'failed all 4 runs after passing earlier', recorded undiagnosed) because whether the crawl beat the next disconnect depended on machine load. Fixed in deploy/scripts/sqlserver-init.sh: both the app database and the Keycloak database are set AUTO_CLOSE OFF behind an is_auto_close_on guard so re-runs are a clean no-op (unlike RCSI this option needs no exclusive access, so no ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE). The U3 gate sets it on its scratch database too, so the spike now exercises the configuration we actually ship. Verified: full spike re-run 17 passed / 0 failed, crawl completing in ~6 seconds.

title: The cloud compose file requests a web image tag that CI never publishes — the first deploy pinned to a commit would fail pulling web, on the box, mid-deploy. deploy/docker-compose.cloud.yml used a single ${ACMP_IMAGE_TAG} for all four ACMP images, but api, worker and sqlserver-fts are environment-AGNOSTIC and published as a plain <sha> while `web` is NOT: ADR-0037 bakes VITE_OIDC_AUTHORITY into the bundle at build time, so P24 publishes web:<sha>-uat and web:<sha>-prod and there is NO plain web:<sha>. Setting ACMP_IMAGE_TAG=<sha> therefore resolved web to a tag that does not exist. Verified against the LIVE registry before fixing: list-images on acmp/web returns exactly <sha>-uat and <sha>-prod, and describe-images for the plain <sha> answers ImageNotFoundException; docker manifest inspect confirms the other three resolve and web:<sha> does not. This is structural rather than a typo — a single shared tag variable CANNOT express a topology in which one image is per-environment by design, so it could never have worked. It is a seam defect: P21 wrote the compose line before P24 chose per-environment web images and the two slices were never reconciled, which is the same class as SL-024's 'consumed by promote.sh' drift and P23's restore.sh pointing at a container ADR-0036 had deleted. The comment sitting immediately below the offending line already documented the -uat/-prod scheme, so the file contradicted itself. It survived because the CLOUD topology had NO CI validation of any kind — the compose job validates docker-compose.yml, the on-prem file, and never referenced docker-compose.cloud.yml. Found by inspection while preparing the first local boot of the cloud stack (option C3), BEFORE any instance was paid for. Fixed: web now reads ${ACMP_WEB_TAG:-${ACMP_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}}, keeping the local build path working while requiring an explicit per-environment tag in cloud; .env.cloud.example documents ACMP_WEB_TAG with the reason. Guarded: ci.yml now config-validates the cloud compose AND runs scripts/check-cloud-images.mjs, which pins both halves of the contract — that compose reads ACMP_WEB_TAG for web and ACMP_IMAGE_TAG for the other three, and that the CI publish job still tags web with both -uat and -prod while publishing the others unsuffixed. The guard was itself tested by re-introducing the bug (fails, exit 1, names the fix) and restoring it (passes).

title: Seq crash-loops on the shipped SEQ_FIRSTRUN_ADMINPASSWORDHASH placeholder, and NOTHING notices — the cloud stack reports fully healthy with observability dead. Seq requires that variable to be a Base-64 salted hash and aborts with System.FormatException 'The input is not a valid Base-64 string' on anything else, including the literal CHANGE_ME that deploy/.env.cloud.example ships. An operator who copies the template and misses that one line gets a container in an endless restart loop. The severity is not the crash, it is that the crash is INVISIBLE: api declares `depends_on: seq: {condition: service_started}`, and service_started is satisfied by a container that started and then died, so a restart-looping Seq never blocks or fails anything downstream. On the first ever boot of the cloud stack, api, web and keycloak all reported HEALTHY while Seq was in Restarting(1) — the deployment looks green and there is no log aggregation at all, which is precisely the state you cannot diagnose your way out of. Same silent-degradation family as DEF-018 (search returns nothing, API logs clean) and DEF-017 (backups never written, deployment looks backed up). It exists only in the CLOUD path: the on-prem .env.example leaves the variable commented out and runs Seq unauthenticated, which is why no previous stack ever hit it. Found by option C3, the first end-to-end boot of docker-compose.cloud.yml, before any instance was paid for. FIXED in deploy/scripts/gen-secrets.sh, which already runs before every compose up: it now rejects a non-Base-64 value with the exact remediation (docker run --rm datalust/seq config hash) and notes that leaving it unset runs Seq without authentication for dev. Validated only when set, so the on-prem path is unaffected. Tested across all three cases — CHANGE_ME exits 1 with the message, a real generated hash exits 0, unset exits 0 — and then proven end to end by regenerating a real hash and recreating the container, which came up healthy.
custom_attributes: {"slice": "SL-021", "found_by": "C3 first end-to-end boot of the cloud stack", "location": "deploy/scripts/gen-secrets.sh, deploy/.env.cloud.example", "mechanism": "depends_on service_started is satisfied by a crash-looping container"}

title: MinioFileStore reported SUCCESS for uploads S3 refused — silent data loss in the running product. FIXED by upgrading the Minio SDK 6.0.3 -> 6.0.5, NOT by the client rewrite first assumed. Measured against real S3 with the least-privilege acmp-uat-app key on 6.0.3: UploadAsync to a bucket that identity cannot write threw NOTHING and returned normally, and ExistsAsync then returned TRUE for an object that was never stored ('upload threw NOTHING | ExistsAsync returned True | Exists threw NOTHING'). S3 was always correct and isolation was always intact — the AWS CLI answers, for the identical identity/bucket/action, 'AccessDenied ... user/acmp-uat-app is not authorized to perform: s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::acmp-prod-recordings/...', and an admin list-objects-v2 confirmed nothing was written; AC-083 never moved. The fault was the client swallowing permission errors on BOTH PutObject and StatObject, which in production means a refused upload reaches the caller as stored: 201 from the API, success in the UI, no file. It also falsified, in writing, the comment inside EnsureBucketAsync claiming 'PutObject immediately after is the real authority and its own failure surfaces to the caller'. TWO WRONG TURNS, both recorded because the reasoning matters more than the patch. First, a post-write ExistsAsync guard was written, tested and REVERTED — it inherits the same blindness since StatObject swallows the denial too, and a guard that cannot fail is worse than none because it manufactures confidence. Second, the recorded remedy was 'the AWSSDK.S3 fallback P22 deferred', a client rewrite touching every file operation in the product; before doing that the cheapest rung was tried instead — the pinned SDK was 6.0.3 and 6.0.5 existed. The bump fixes it: the isolation regression test now throws on the refused write, and the full integration suite passes 43/43 including the Testcontainers-MinIO on-prem path (container start confirmed in the Testcontainers log, so the on-prem adapter is genuinely exercised, not skipped). CONSEQUENTIAL CHANGE, not optional: 6.0.5 also fixed the AWSS3Endpoints rewriting that P22 documented, so presigned URLs now use the CONFIGURED endpoint (https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) instead of the legacy global host (https://s3.amazonaws.com). ACMP_MEDIA_ORIGIN, the compose default and the nginx CSP media-src comment were all updated to match, and both the offline and live tests re-pinned — leaving them would have blocked <video> playback in the browser with nothing in the API logs, which is the exact silent shape the P22 finding warned about.

title: Cron backups silently skipped the off-instance S3 copy, so NFR-058 was unmet with no error anywhere. deploy/scripts/crontab.example ran backup.sh with NO ACMP_ENV_FILE set, so backup.sh defaulted ENV_FILE to deploy/.env -- a file the cloud bootstrap never creates, because 08-bootstrap-box.sh writes deploy/.env.cloud. The source line ended in `|| true`, so the miss was swallowed rather than reported; ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET was consequently unset, the guard was false, and the `aws s3 cp` leg was skipped entirely. The .bak files were still written locally, so the backup APPEARED to succeed with a clean cron log -- the backups simply never left the instance they were backing up, which is precisely what NFR-058 exists to prevent. Same silent-degradation family as DEF-017, DEF-018, DEF-020 and DEF-023. It bit only the CLOUD path: on-prem the operator creates deploy/.env by hand, so the default resolved. FIXED with remedy (c), both ends, as recommended. crontab.example now sets ACMP_ENV_FILE=/opt/acmp/deploy/.env.cloud at the top; and backup.sh REFUSES to run when its env file is absent instead of falling through to defaults, which fixes the whole class rather than this instance. The refusal has one narrow, explicit escape: a caller that has genuinely configured everything in the environment already has ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET set, and that is the only case where a missing file is not a misconfiguration. A genuinely bucket-less run (local drills) now NAMES the skip in the log, because the original defect was invisible precisely because it looked identical to a normal run. EVIDENCE, CORRECTED 2026-08-08 -- the original wording of this row overstated what was verified and is fixed here rather than left standing. What IS evidenced: backup.sh was run on the box through `env -i` with only ACMP_ENV_FILE set, exactly the stripped environment cron provides, both databases were backed up, and a SEPARATE `aws s3 ls` confirmed the objects landed -- s3://acmp-uat-backups/sql/Acmp_20260807_145954.bak (7,327,744 B) and keycloak_20260807_145954.bak (12,111,872 B). That proves backup.sh works and that the S3 leg fires under cron's environment. What was NOT true, and was claimed here until this correction: that 'the crontab was installed from crontab.example'. It was not. Amazon Linux 2023 ships no cron at all, so `crontab /tmp/ct` failed with `command not found` in the same batch -- and because `aws ssm send-command` joins its command list with no set -e, the failure was swallowed, the following commands ran, and the invocation still reported Success. The manual backup evidence was real but it was evidence for backup.sh, never for the SCHEDULE, which did not exist on that box. See DEF-026, which found this and installs cronie in the bootstrap.

title: NOBODY CAN LOG IN TO A CLOUD ENVIRONMENT: the Keycloak realm export registers only dev and ngrok redirect URIs, so the SPA's PKCE hand-off is rejected — and every health signal stays green. deploy/keycloak/realm-export.json declared acmp-web's redirectUris as localhost:8088, localhost:5173 and two ngrok hosts, with NO cloud hostname anywhere, and deploy/docker-compose.cloud.yml mounts it verbatim with no per-environment substitution. The SPA started a correct PKCE flow and Keycloak answered 'Invalid parameter: redirect_uri'. Prod was identical. SEVERITY WAS DRIVEN BY THE INVISIBILITY, as with DEF-017/018/020: all six containers healthy, three one-shots exited 0, valid Let's Encrypt certificate, correct external issuer, /api/ correctly 401 — Keycloak WAS running properly and simply refused the one redirect URI the application uses. The bootstrap's nine assertions, the local boot gate's twenty-seven and every external curl probe passed on a box no human could enter, because none performed a browser round-trip. STRUCTURAL, the same seam class as DEF-019: realm-export.json was authored for the dev/ngrok topology BEFORE ADR-0037 chose per-environment subdomains, and a single shared realm file cannot express a hostname that is per-environment by design. FIXED (remedy (b), as recommended) in deploy/keycloak/reconcile.sh, the keycloak-config one-shot that already reconciles the realm over kcadm: ensure_web_origin REPLACES redirectUris and webOrigins from ACMP_WEB_ORIGIN, which ONLY docker-compose.cloud.yml sets (from KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN, the single browser-facing origin in the cloud topology where the SPA and Keycloak share an origin under /kc/). The dev compose deliberately does not pass it — there KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN is keycloak.localhost:8085 while the SPA is on localhost:8088, so it is NOT the SPA origin and using it would break dev; unset means the block no-ops. Replace rather than append: assignment is what makes re-runs idempotent, and a public OIDC client in cloud has no business accepting localhost redirects. The script READS THE VALUE BACK rather than trusting kcadm's exit code, because this is a defect that every green check missed. post.logout.redirect.uris needed no patching — it is now the literal '+' in the export, Keycloak's 'whatever redirectUris allows', which is environment-independent and sidesteps kcadm's dotted-key path splitting entirely. NOTE the export reaches only a FIRST import, so a realm created before that edit keeps its old list. VERIFIED THE WAY THE DEFECT DEMANDED, not with a health check. Negative-tested on the local cloud boot gate first, free: with the fix the configured origin gets the login form (HTTP 200) while http://localhost:8088 — a URI the committed export DOES register — is refused (HTTP 400), proving the reconcile genuinely replaced and that the gate's grep matches the real Keycloak error text. Then on a from-scratch UAT box (i-05085d458d886dc08) all four seeded accounts (chairman, secretary, member, auditor) completed a real browser PKCE login through the repo's own Playwright, were forced through UPDATE_PASSWORD, and landed JIT-provisioned with the CORRECT role via POST /api/members/me. GUARDED: cloud-stack-boot.sh now drives the exact authorization request the SPA builds and asserts Keycloak serves a login form rather than the redirect_uri error, so this defect class is detectable without a browser — which is the gap this defect documents. Its second observation, the CSP blocking Keycloak's inline scripts, was assessed and raised as its own row: see DEF-025 (it also uncovered that X-Frame-Options DENY was blocking the silent-renew iframe).

title: certbot-deploy-hook.sh was committed 100644, so certbot ABORTED the whole certonly run and a fresh box got NO certificate — while the SSM invocation reported Success. certbot execs a --deploy-hook directly rather than through an interpreter, so a non-executable hook is refused outright with 'hook command deploy exists, but is not executable' and the entire certificate issuance is abandoned. On the AC-075 rebuild (i-05085d458d886dc08) the site therefore served CN=ACMP-PLACEHOLDER-DO-NOT-TRUST, which is exactly the state deploy/scripts/certbot-deploy-hook.sh's placeholder naming exists to make unmissable. SEVERITY IS THE INVISIBILITY, the same family as DEF-017/018/020/022/023: the SSM run answered Success because AWS-RunShellScript joins the command list into one script with no set -e, so the exit status is the LAST command's — `systemctl is-active certbot-renew.timer` returning `active` masked a certbot that had never issued anything. The renewal timer was genuinely enabled, which made the run look MORE convincing, not less. Found only because runbook section 6 phrases its verification as 'read the certificate subject from off the box' rather than 'did the command exit 0'. Root cause is a git file mode: every other deploy script is invoked as `bash <script>` and does not care, so nothing else surfaced it. Class swept — the only two scripts invoked WITHOUT an explicit interpreter are this hook (by certbot) and backup.sh (by cron), and backup.sh was already 100755. A SECOND, SEPARATE section-6 finding recorded with it: the documented certbot command cannot run over the only access path this deployment has. title: Keycloak's own pages inherited the SPA's security headers under /kc/, breaking its login theme's inline scripts and BLOCKING the silent-renew iframe — so every session would have dropped at token expiry instead of renewing, with no error anywhere. This is DEF-023's second observation, recorded there as unassessed and now ASSESSED on the rebuilt box. nginx sets the security headers at SERVER level in both cloud-443.conf.template and default.conf.template, and add_header therefore applies them to everything proxied under /kc/ as well as to the SPA. Two of them are actively wrong for Keycloak's pages. (1) `script-src 'self'` blocks the login theme's INLINE scripts: 7 CSP console violations were observed on every one of four logins. The form still submits, so it is not fatal today, but the theme runs degraded and anything script-driven (password-strength hints, the locale switcher, WebAuthn) is one Keycloak release from breaking with nothing in our logs. (2) `X-Frame-Options: DENY` is emitted ON TOP of Keycloak's own SAMEORIGIN, and conflicting XFO values resolve to deny. The SPA sets automaticSilentRenew with no silent_redirect_uri (src/Acmp.Web/src/auth/authConfig.ts), so oidc-client-ts renews through a hidden SAME-ORIGIN iframe pointed at /kc/ — which deny blocks. MEASURED RATHER THAN REASONED, which matters because the first version of this finding was an inference from a header dump: the login probe now appends that iframe and reports whether it loads, and on the deployed box it was BLOCKED before the fix and loads after. The symptom would never have been an error — users would simply be logged out when the access token expired, which reads as flakiness rather than a defect. FIXED by giving /kc/ its own add_header block in BOTH nginx templates, kept identical: Keycloak owns Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options for its own pages (it already sets XFO SAMEORIGIN, Referrer-Policy no-referrer, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff and its own CSP), and we keep only HSTS and Permissions-Policy, which it does not set. The non-merging behaviour of add_header is the trap here and is called out in both files: this block REPLACES the server-level set for /kc/, so anything wanted there must be listed there. GUARDED: cloud-stack-boot.sh now asserts, on a /kc/ path, that our CSP is absent, that XFO deny is absent, and that HSTS survives — the block was otherwise unguarded in exactly the way DEF-019 and DEF-023 both were. VERIFIED after deploy: /kc/ returns Keycloak's SAMEORIGIN with no CSP from us, HSTS and Permissions-Policy present, the SPA's own / still carries all six headers (AC-081 posture intact), the iframe loads for all four users and zero CSP violations are reported.

title: Amazon Linux 2023 ships NO cron, so the backup SCHEDULE never existed on any provisioned box -- NFR-056 and NFR-058 unmet while everything looked healthy. title: AC-076's ORIGINAL method could not work: the e2e suite's global-setup needs exactly the two Keycloak endpoints the 443 listener deliberately 404s for AC-081. RESOLVED 2026-08-09 by amending the AC (OQ-066), after the remedy was executed end to end. THE ORIGINAL FINDING, unchanged and still correct as a statement about the original text: AC-076 said to run the Playwright suite with E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL=https://uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev/kc. That suite's global-setup (src/Acmp.Web/e2e/global-setup.ts) seeds its deterministic e2e-* users through the Keycloak ADMIN REST API, which needs a master-realm token from ${KC_BASE}/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token and then calls ${KC_BASE}/admin/realms/acmp/... . deploy/nginx/cloud-443.conf.template denies BOTH by design -- `location ~ ^/kc/(admin|realms/master)(/|$) { return 404; }` -- because everything under /kc/ is publicly reachable the moment 443 exists, and that would put the realm-administration UI and the master realm on the public internet next to the login page. MEASURED against the live host: /kc/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token returned 404 and /kc/admin/realms/acmp/users returned 404, while /kc/realms/acmp/.well-known/openid-configuration returned 200. A SEAM defect of the same class as DEF-019 and DEF-023: the AC assumed the suite points at a Keycloak it can administer, which is true of the disposable e2e stack it was designed for, and the deny rule was chosen later for the public cloud listener -- nothing reconciled the two. HOW IT WAS RESOLVED, and it is worth separating the two halves. THE MECHANISM: option (b), an SSM port-forward, executed with ZERO code change. session-manager-plugin needed no installation -- the winget/MSI route wants Program Files and stalls on a UAC prompt, but AWS's SessionManagerPlugin.zip carries a nested package.zip whose bin/session-manager-plugin.exe runs standalone, and `aws ssm start-session` only needs it on PATH. `AWS-StartPortForwardingSession portNumber=80,localPortNumber=8085` opened first try against i-07ac28ac2fedab921, which also settled that acmp-admin holds ssm:StartSession (a different IAM action from the ssm:SendCommand used elsewhere in this project). Through that tunnel, against the nginx 8080 server block which carries no /kc/ deny: /kc/realms/master/.well-known/openid-configuration -> 200 and /kc/admin/realms/acmp/users -> 401 -- REACHABLE and merely unauthenticated, proving both that nginx is not denying it there and that Keycloak's `hostname strict` does not reject a localhost Host header on the admin REST API. With the bootstrap admin credential the master-realm token issued (773-char JWT) and the admin API answered 200, listing the real ACMP realm roles. global-setup then seeded e2e-secretary, e2e-chairman and e2e-member over the tunnel while the browser drove the PUBLIC host, and the suite ran (AV-108). The same three paths on the public 443 listener returned 200/404/404 in the same minute, so AC-081's posture was re-evidenced rather than weakened. THE GOVERNANCE HALF: a working procedure alone would have left the AC still saying something impossible, so AC-076's statement was amended per OQ-066 to name the port-forward. That is what closes this defect -- the package and reality now agree. Options (a) an out-of-band seeder and (c) relaxing the deny were both left unused; (c) remains rejected as a direct security regression. WHAT THE RESOLUTION DELIBERATELY PRESERVES: seed-users.sh gained no password bypass, so its temporary-password + UPDATE_PASSWORD behaviour still holds for CON-007/CON-009 and attributed voting; the /kc/ deny is untouched; and the fixed-password e2e-* accounts the suite creates were DELETED from the realm after the run (HTTP 204 each), since their password is committed in e2e/users.ts and UAT's 443 is open to 0.0.0.0/0 -- that cleanup is now written into the amended AC as a standing requirement rather than left to memory.

title: SchedulePage accepted a submit before the chair list had loaded, and failed SILENTLY: onSubmit's `!chair` guard returned with no message, no request and the button still enabled. ROOT CAUSE ISOLATED AND FIXED 2026-08-09 (commit ed74130). REPRODUCED BY EXPERIMENT, not inferred. A probe logged in as the seeded secretary against live UAT, opened /meetings/new, WAITED SIX SECONDS, filled the form exactly as core-loop.spec.ts does and clicked Schedule: POST /api/meetings was issued and meeting MTG-2026-001 was created. The identical probe with the wait REMOVED -- i.e. behaving exactly as the spec does -- reproduced the failure precisely: GET /api/members had not even been sent, the chair control still read 'Loading members...', the click produced NO request at all, and NO error element rendered anywhere on the page. One variable changed, opposite outcomes. TWO FAULTS, NOT ONE. (1) The form accepted a submit while useMembers() was still loading, so activeMembers was empty and the `!chair` guard returned early and silently with the button still enabled. (2) The one error that would have explained it is DERIVED state, not latched, so it disappeared the instant the query resolved -- which is why the original failure screenshot showed a perfectly valid form with 'chairman Seeded' already selected and no error at all: by the time Playwright captured it 180 seconds later the data had arrived, and the diagnostic had been overwritten by the recovery. Compounding it, chairError tested `!effectiveChairId`, strictly WEAKER than the guard's `!chair` lookup, so the two could disagree with nothing shown. WHY CI NEVER CAUGHT IT, and why this is a product defect rather than a test artifact: on localhost the members query always wins the race against the test; over the internet it does not. A real user on a slow connection who clicks Schedule promptly gets the same silence, on a governance-critical form. The e2e workflow runs green on the same spec against the local compose stack, so no amount of CI would have surfaced this -- AC-076 found a defect that 140 green frontend test files and a green e2e workflow could not, which is precisely the argument for AC-076 existing. FIX: `chair` is resolved ONCE in render scope so the guard and the message derive from the same lookup and cannot disagree, and Schedule is DISABLED while members are loading -- `disabled` rather than `loading`, because the button is not busy, the form is not ready, and the chair field already says so. Disabling is also what lets the e2e suite pass with NO change to the spec, since Playwright waits for an enabled button and the race therefore cannot occur. Two regression tests added: Schedule disabled while loading, and the chair error shown when the list resolves empty. Frontend 140 test files green, coverage 99.64% against the 95% floor. RETRACTION OF A FALSE LEAD THIS ROW CARRIED IN ITS FIRST VERSION: it asserted that 'GET /api/members appears NOWHERE in the access log for the run' and offered that as the first thread to pull. THE EVIDENCE DID NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM -- the grep behind it ended in `tail -n 8`, and every one of those eight lines was the frequently-polling POST /api/members/me, so any earlier GET fell outside the window. The honest statement was 'I did not check', and the request does in fact happen normally once the page has settled. A claim of ABSENCE is never supportable by a truncated search. NOT YET DEPLOYED: ci.yml publishes images only on a push to main, so this fix sits on a branch and the running UAT box is unchanged. AC-076 cannot go Met until the branch is merged, /acmp/uat/env re-pinned to the new tags and the box re-bootstrapped.

title: DELETING the e2e-* Keycloak users between runs permanently DUPLICATES their CommitteeMember rows, because app-side identity is the Keycloak sub and member rows cannot be removed. FIXED 2026-08-09. WHAT HAPPENED: after the first AC-076 run the three fixed-password e2e-* Keycloak users were DELETED, for a sound reason -- their password is committed in e2e/users.ts and UAT's 443 is open to 0.0.0.0/0. On the next run global-setup re-created them, Keycloak minted NEW `sub` values, and JIT provisioning created a SECOND CommitteeMember row for each. MEASURED: GET /api/members returned 10 rows where 7 were expected -- 'E2E Chairman' x2, 'E2E Member' x2, 'E2E Secretary' x2, all six active -- and core-loop.spec.ts could not pass, because its owner picker uses getByRole('option', {name: 'E2E Member', exact: true}) which then matched two elements and failed Playwright strict mode. THE ROOT TENSION WAS REAL AND BOTH SIDES WERE CORRECT. Security says delete a known-password account reachable from the internet. Repeatability says do not: P17b fixed all identity to member.keycloakUserId precisely so identity is stable and attributable, and the audit chain is immutable, so a CommitteeMember row can be DEACTIVATED but never removed. Deleting the upstream identity therefore orphans a row that outlives it. RESOLVED IN TWO PARTS. PREVENTION: DISABLE the Keycloak user (`PUT /admin/realms/acmp/users/{id}` with {"enabled": false}) instead of deleting it -- a disabled account cannot authenticate, so the risk is removed just as completely, and the sub survives so the next run re-enables the SAME identity and duplicates nothing. All three are now managed this way, and AC-076's cleanup clause was corrected from 'deleted' to 'disabled' so the AC stops prescribing what caused this. REMEDIATION of the rows already created: the orphans were identified precisely rather than guessed -- the two rows in each pair share display name, role AND email, and only the sub distinguishes them, so each row's keycloakUserId was matched against the subs still present in the realm. The three whose sub was gone were deactivated through the sanctioned endpoint POST /api/members/{publicId}/deactivate as an Administrator: 4126bdc9-b6d8-4963-9db3-2b8d1b4b5aa0 (E2E Chairman, orphan sub b0bf51fb), 6432bcce-fe70-44d6-9265-9e8d03360849 (E2E Member, orphan sub aba62130), 86815220-6154-4af9-a766-3bcfe3714896 (E2E Secretary, orphan sub a309db7d) -- HTTP 204 each. Deactivating a member is an ordinary governance action, not data repair; no database was touched and no file on the box was edited. VERIFIED: /api/members now returns 8 active rows with NO duplicate display names (the eighth is acmp-admin's own row, JIT-provisioned when it first signed in), and the full AC-076 suite subsequently ran 7 passed / 0 failed against live UAT -- see AV-115. NOTE ON WHAT IT COST TO CLOSE: the deactivate endpoint is gated on Policies.AdminUsers, and reading role-mappings for all eight realm users showed that ONLY acmp-admin holds the Administrator realm role. A password had to be set on that account -- the environment's sole administrative credential -- which was done under explicit operator delegation and is recorded rather than left implicit. METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING: immutability means cleanup is never symmetric with creation. Deleting upstream does not delete downstream, it ORPHANS it, and the orphan outlives the reason for the deletion.

title: THE ENTIRE BUDGET ALERT CHAIN HAS NEVER BEEN ABLE TO DELIVER: the acmp-budget-alerts SNS topic never granted budgets.amazonaws.com permission to publish, so every budget notification is rejected while the budget still reports itself as armed and firing. Found 2026-08-09 by an out-of-band email from budgets@costalerts.amazonaws.com: 'we are unable to successfully publish to this SNS topic... if you do not adjust your SNS topic permissions, it is likely that budget notifications will not be sent to your SNS topic subscribers.' ROOT CAUSE, confirmed by reading the live policy: deploy/aws/00-account.sh creates the topic and subscribes the operator's email, but never sets a topic policy, so the topic carried only AWS's DEFAULT policy -- a single statement with Principal {"AWS": "*"} gated on Condition AWS:SourceOwner = the account. That covers IAM principals INSIDE the account. AWS Budgets does not publish as an account principal; it publishes as the SERVICE principal budgets.amazonaws.com, which cannot satisfy AWS:SourceOwner. Every publish attempt was therefore denied. WHY THIS WENT UNNOTICED FOR SIX DAYS, and it is the most important part of this row: THE FAILURE IS INVISIBLE FROM THE BUDGET SIDE. Budgets evaluates the threshold and updates the notification's state regardless of whether the publish succeeds. So `describe-budget-actions-for-budget` shows both actions STANDBY at 100%, `describe-notifications-for-budget` shows notifications at 50/80/100% correctly configured, `list-subscriptions-by-topic` shows a CONFIRMED email subscription with a real ARN -- and on a genuine threshold crossing the notification duly flips OK -> ALARM. Every observable on the control plane says the alerting works. The only signal that it does not is the SNS topic's own NumberOfMessagesPublished metric sitting at ZERO, and an email AWS sends out-of-band to the account contact. BLAST RADIUS IS THE WHOLE COST GUARDRAIL, not just the test notification that exposed it. The 50%, 80% and 100% ACTUAL notifications on the $60/month budget could never have been delivered either. The operator would have received NO warning at 50% or 80%, and no notification when the 100% brake fired. NOT AFFECTED: the budget ACTIONS themselves. The IAM deny and the SSM STOP_EC2_INSTANCES action are executed by the budgets service through the acmp-budget-action execution role, independent of SNS delivery, so the brake would still have engaged -- silently. The realistic failure mode was therefore an operator who receives nothing, notices nothing, and then discovers the situation by being denied ec2:RunInstances. FIXED at both ends. Live: a policy with two statements is now on the topic -- the original DefaultAccountAccess statement preserved verbatim, plus AllowBudgetsToPublish granting Service budgets.amazonaws.com the SNS:Publish action on this topic, conditioned on aws:SourceAccount = 565393059398. That condition is the confused-deputy guard and is not optional: the topic ARN is guessable, and without it any AWS customer's budget could publish into this alert channel. Read back after applying; both statements present. In source: 00-account.sh now sets that policy immediately after subscribing the email, so a fresh account cannot reproduce this. VERIFICATION IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED YET. The 2% notification that exposed this was already in ALARM, and an alert with no state left to change gives Budgets nothing to re-send, so its continued silence would prove nothing. It was deleted and replaced with a 2.3% threshold ($1.38 against $1.286 actual) which sits in OK and will cross on ordinary spend, producing a genuine OK -> ALARM transition AFTER the policy fix. Delivery is confirmed only when NumberOfMessagesPublished on acmp-budget-alerts goes non-zero against its long-standing zero baseline. METHOD NOTE WORTH KEEPING: this defect is exactly why AC-085 leg 1 was written as 'a threshold notification has been OBSERVED TO ARRIVE' rather than 'a notification is configured'. Every configuration check passed for six days. Had the softer reading been accepted -- and NotificationState: ALARM was available and tempting -- the AC would have been marked Met over a cost guardrail that could not raise an alarm.

title: The acmp-uat-cpu-credits-low alarm had NO alarm actions: it changed state and told nobody. Found 2026-08-09 by a deliberate sweep for the DEF-030 CLASS -- controls that look armed on every check while their notification path does not exist. FOUND BY INSPECTION, unlike DEF-030 which needed an email from AWS. `describe-alarms` returned AlarmActions: [], OKActions: [], InsufficientDataActions: [] with ActionsEnabled: true, and deploy/aws/07-launch.sh confirms it was created that way -- the put-metric-alarm call passed no --alarm-actions at all. So the alarm was never wired to anything; this is not configuration drift. AN ALARM WITH NO ACTION IS A DASHBOARD WIDGET, NOT A CONTROL. It evaluates correctly, transitions correctly, and is fully visible to anyone who thinks to run describe-alarms -- which is exactly nobody, at the moment it matters. This is the third instance of one shape in this project: DEF-023's health probes passed on a box nobody could log into, DEF-030's budget notifications changed state while every publish was denied, and here an alarm fires into the void. In all three the observable that was being watched was healthy while the capability it stood for was absent. WHAT IT DOES NOT INVALIDATE, stated precisely because the temptation runs the other way: AC-084's clause is 'the CPUCreditBalance alarm is not tripped', which is a claim about the alarm's STATE. That state is real, was read directly, and was watched to clear at 50.09 credits and hold OK through an e2e run. AV-112 and AV-113 stand unaltered. What was missing is the alarm's operational value -- nobody would have been TOLD -- which is a defect in the control, not in the evidence for the criterion. FIXED in 07-launch.sh and live: --alarm-actions and --ok-actions both pointed at the acmp-budget-alerts topic. That topic is reused deliberately rather than creating a second one: it already carries the operator's CONFIRMED email subscription, so this needs no new infrastructure and no second confirmation click. --ok-actions is included so recovery is visible too; an ALARM email with no matching all-clear gets mentally filed as 'still broken'. VERIFIED END TO END, which DEF-030 could not be: `set-alarm-state` forces a real transition on demand, so the whole chain was tested rather than reasoned about. Two forced ALARM->OK cycles produced NumberOfMessagesPublished 2.0 and 2.0 in consecutive 5-minute buckets, NumberOfNotificationsDelivered 2.0 and 2.0, NumberOfNotificationsFailed 0.0 -- against a baseline that had been ZERO for the entire session. Real emails were delivered to the operator. A CORRECTION I MADE TO MYSELF IN THE SAME TEST, recorded because the wrong version was live for four minutes: after the FIRST fire showed no datapoints I inferred that CloudWatch was blocked the way Budgets was, and added an AllowCloudWatchAlarmsToPublish statement to the topic policy. The data then showed the first fire HAD published -- its 2.0 landed in the 13:20 bucket, before the policy change at 13:25 -- so the initial zero was simply metric lag, which I had flagged as a caveat and then failed to wait out. CloudWatch alarms publish fine under the default account policy; only Budgets, as a service principal that cannot satisfy AWS:SourceOwner, needed an explicit grant. The unnecessary statement was REVERTED rather than kept as harmless belt-and-braces, because a redundant Allow whose comment asserts a false necessity teaches the next reader something untrue. The live policy and 00-account.sh both carry two statements. SEPARATE GAP FOUND IN THE SAME SWEEP, not fixed and not a defect row: backup failures have no alerting path either. deploy/scripts/crontab.example redirects output to /var/log/acmp-backup.log and its own comment says a non-zero exit 'is where an alert hooks in (mail, Seq webhook, etc.)' -- i.e. the hook is a placeholder and nothing is wired. A failed nightly backup is therefore silent unless somebody reads the log. That is DISCLOSED in the file rather than hidden, which is why it is recorded here rather than raised as a defect, but it is worth an operator decision now that the SNS topic demonstrably delivers: AC-080 is Met on a regime that runs unattended, and an unattended regime that fails quietly is the failure mode this AC exists to prevent. THIRD CHECK IN THE SWEEP CAME BACK CLEAN: the nightly hash-chain integrity sweep (Acmp.Worker, Cron.Daily(3), ADR-0030) DOES have a designed reporting path -- IntegrityVerifier logs a high-importance event and emits a durable AuditEvent on detection, so the detection is itself tamper-evident and extends the chain it checked. No gap there.

title: Backup failures were SILENT: two comments asserted alerting that had never existed, and the hook they pointed at was an unfilled placeholder. Fixed and verified end to end 2026-08-09. THE FALSE CLAIMS, both in code that a reader would reasonably trust: deploy/scripts/crontab.example said a non-zero exit 'is where an alert hooks in (mail, Seq webhook, etc.)', and backup.sh said 'any failure aborts the run (cron alerts on the non-zero exit)'. NEITHER WAS TRUE. The crontab lines redirect stdout AND stderr to /var/log/acmp-backup.log, so cron has nothing to mail; and Amazon Linux 2023 ships no MTA, so cron would have had nowhere to mail it even without the redirect. A failed nightly backup was therefore visible only to somebody who thought to read the log, which is nobody, at 02:00. This is the FOURTH instance of one shape in this project -- DEF-023's health probes passing on a box nobody could log into, DEF-030's budget notifications changing state while every publish was denied, DEF-031's alarm with no action, and now a backup regime that cannot report its own failure. In each case the observable being watched was healthy while the capability it stood for was absent. WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: AC-080 is Met on a regime that runs UNATTENDED, and NFR-058's whole point is that a backup exists off-instance when it is needed. A backup that stops working and says nothing is indistinguishable from one that works, right up until a restore is attempted. FIX. backup.sh publishes failures to ACMP_ALERT_TOPIC_ARN from an EXIT trap, with an ERR trap capturing the failing line number and command so the alert names the actual failure rather than just 'it broke'. Three design choices are deliberate. (1) SKIPPED-BUT-LOUD when ACMP_ALERT_TOPIC_ARN is unset, exactly matching the ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET treatment: DEF-022 was a capability that skipped itself in silence, and the fix for that is not to introduce a new silent skip. (2) The alert NEVER MASKS the original failure -- its own errors are caught, logged with the precise IAM statement to check, and the script still exits with the backup's exit code. (3) It reuses the acmp-budget-alerts topic rather than creating a second one, because that topic already carries the operator's CONFIRMED email subscription; the name is narrower than the use, and if a second channel is ever wanted the note in .env.cloud.example says to create acmp-ops-alerts and repoint. Both false comments were corrected rather than left to mislead. IAM: 03-iam.sh now grants sns:Publish scoped to that one topic, applied live to acmp-uat-instance and acmp-prod-instance by patching the LIVE policy document rather than rewriting it from a template. Without it the alert would have failed at 02:00 and logged its failure into the same log nobody reads -- the defect reproducing itself one layer down. VERIFICATION, and the first attempt at it was itself a check that could not fail. Four paths were first driven locally against a stubbed aws CLI: publish-on-failure, topic-unset, publish-itself-fails, and success. Then on the box: the instance role was proven able to publish (assumed-role/acmp-uat-instance returned a real MessageId). THEN A LIVE FAILURE DRILL -- and the first version of it passed for the wrong reason. Passing ACMP_DB_NAMES=<bogus> on the command line changed nothing, because backup.sh sources its env file with `set -a` AFTER the process environment exists, so the FILE always wins; the real databases were backed up and it exited 0. Rewritten to override the env FILE instead, the drill produced a genuine failure: 'Msg 911 ... Database definitely_not_a_database does not exist', backup.sh exited 1, the trap reported 'FAILED (exit 1) at line 131' with the failing sqlcmd invocation, and published. DELIVERY WAS CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY of the script's own success line, from SNS metrics: 1 published, 1 delivered, 0 failed. SIDE FINDING, worth knowing before writing a config override: backup.sh's header says 'Config (env or deploy/.env)' and its own on-prem usage example exports ACMP_DB_NAMES on the command line. That example only works where the env file does not set the variable. In cloud it does, so the file silently wins.

title: check-backup-freshness.sh reproduced DEF-022 within an hour of being written: it swallowed a missing env file and exited 0 reporting 'nothing to check'. Found and fixed 2026-08-09, before it was trusted. WHAT HAPPENED: the script's first version sourced its env file only `[ -f ]` it existed and otherwise carried on. Run without ACMP_ENV_FILE on a cloud box -- where the file is deploy/.env.cloud, not deploy/.env -- ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET stayed empty, and the script exited 0 with 'ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET is unset - nothing to check'. THIS IS DEF-022 EXACTLY. DEF-022 was the defect where backup.sh defaulted to deploy/.env, the miss was swallowed, ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET stayed unset, and the off-instance copy was skipped ENTIRELY while the run reported success. I rebuilt that defect inside the very script written to detect the absence of backups, in the same session in which I catalogued four other silent-control failures, having read backup.sh's own DEF-022 comment while writing it. AND IT IS WORSE HERE THAN IT WAS THERE. backup.sh's swallow produced a backup that existed locally but not off-instance -- bad, but something existed. This script's swallow produces the message 'nothing to check', which is INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM 'backups are fine' to anyone reading the log. A control that actively reassures while doing nothing is worse than no control, because an absent control is at least not trusted. WHY IT SURVIVED WRITING AND REVIEW: under cron it works. crontab.example sets ACMP_ENV_FILE at the top, so both the @reboot and daily lines pass it correctly, and every local test had been run with an explicit ACMP_ENV_FILE or ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET. The defect is reachable only when a human runs the script by hand on the box -- which is precisely what an operator does when investigating whether backups are healthy, i.e. the worst possible moment to be told 'nothing to check'. backup.sh's own comment already names the principle: THE REFUSAL IS THE NET, NOT THE PLAN. FOUND BY RUNNING IT ON THE BOX before trusting the reboot test, rather than by review. That is the only reason it was caught: the plan had been to install the crontab and verify @reboot, and the by-hand run was included solely so that a reboot would not be the script's debut. FIXED, with the same remedy backup.sh received: no env file AND no ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET in the environment is a hard exit 1 naming the cloud path; an env file that exists but sets no bucket is also exit 1, because local-only backups are not backups (NFR-058) and reporting 'nothing to check' would hide that. Regression-checked in both directions -- the exact invocation that previously passed silently now exits 1 with the reason, and the configured path still reports OK. DEPLOYMENT NOTE, recorded rather than glossed: the fix is on main (fcb78c1) but the BOX still carries the pre-fix script from 87b4a8a8. The delta is inert under cron, which is the only way the box runs it, since the crontab supplies ACMP_ENV_FILE -- so the @reboot verification below is unaffected. It lands on the next bootstrap. Stated explicitly because 'the fix is merged' and 'the fix is running' are different claims and this project has been bitten by conflating them.

title: The shell's 'viewing as' badge shows an ARBITRARY role, not the member's primary one -- and the correct value is already being sent and thrown away. Found by the operator on his first production login, 2026-08-10. WHAT HE SAW: a five-role account (Secretary, Reviewer, Auditor, Administrator, Member) rendered 'viewing as auditor'. He expected Secretary, which is correct -- Secretary IS his primary role. THE CAUSE IS ONE LINE. src/Acmp.Web/src/components/shell/SideNav.tsx:24 reads `const primaryRole = roles[0] ?? 'Guest';`. That takes the FIRST ELEMENT OF THE CLAIMS ARRAY in whatever order Keycloak returned the realm role-mappings -- insertion or storage order, not precedence. It is not a primary role by any definition; it is an accident of ordering that happens to be stable enough to look deliberate. For a single-role user it is right by coincidence, which is why it survived every earlier environment: the defect is INVISIBLE until someone holds more than one role, and until 2026-08-10 nobody on any deployed environment did. AND A SECOND BUG ON THE ADJACENT LINE, which is why it rendered in English inside an Arabic UI: SideNav.tsx:31 looked up `t(`roles.${primaryRole}`)`, but the locale defines `role.` -- SINGULAR -- at en.json:884 and ar.json:884 with all eight keys, and there is no top-level `roles` key in either file. The lookup could never resolve, so i18next fell through to its defaultValue and printed the bare lowercase claim string in both languages. Only the first bug was reported; the second is what made it look broken rather than merely wrong. THE RIGHT ANSWER ALREADY EXISTS AND IS ALREADY ON THE WIRE. The backend resolves it properly: ProvisionCurrentUser.cs:42 calls CommitteeRoleResolver.PrimaryRole (highest privilege wins -- lowest CommitteeRole enum value), and MemberProfileDto (ProvisionCurrentUser.cs:20) carries BOTH a singular `Role` (the resolved primary) and `Roles` (the full claim set). The SPA receives it and discards it: AcmpAuthContext.ts:14 exposes only `roles: CommitteeRole[]`, with no singular field, so the frontend re-derives a value the backend had already computed correctly -- and derives it wrong. This is a seam defect rather than a logic defect: two layers each own a notion of 'primary role' and only one of them is right. SEVERITY IS PRESENTATION-ONLY, AND THAT IS WORTH BEING PRECISE ABOUT. No authorization depends on it. CapabilityHandler and AuthorizationBehavior are any-of over the full role set, and navigation is filtered by the same set -- which is why the operator's session correctly showed the Secretary queue, the Audit log AND Administration simultaneously. So nothing is granted or denied wrongly; the label above a correct menu is simply mislabelled. In a governance platform where attribution is the product, telling a Secretary he is acting as an Auditor is still a real problem: it invites him to doubt correct behaviour, or to trust an incorrect one later. RELATED, NOT A DEFECT: there is no production role SWITCHER. `devSetRoles` is documented in AcmpAuthContext.ts:25-26 as 'DEV-only role switcher for the shell preview; undefined in production'. The operator expected to select among his roles; that capability was deliberately not shipped, and whether it should be is a product question rather than a bug.

title: HALF THE WCAG CONTRAST GATE HAS BEEN GRADING THE WRONG PALETTE SINCE THE DAY IT WAS WRITTEN. src/Acmp.Web/src/styles/contrast.test.ts machine-verifies every text/background token pair against WCAG 2.2 AA in BOTH themes -- it exists because jsdom cannot compute rendered colour, so the component axe tests disable the color-contrast rule and this file is the compensating control. Its block() helper located a rule with `css.indexOf(selector)`, then took the next '{' and the next '}'. tokens.css line 4 documents `[data-theme="dark"]` IN ITS OWN HEADER COMMENT. So indexOf matched the PROSE, walked forward to the next opening brace -- which belongs to `:root` -- and returned the LIGHT palette. `const DARK = { ...LIGHT, ...block('[data-theme="dark"]') }` was therefore LIGHT spread over LIGHT, and every assertion in the 'dark' describe block compared light tokens against light tokens. INVISIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION, WHICH IS THE INTERESTING PART. The light palette passes AA, so the mis-parsed gate was green -- and a green gate is indistinguishable from a working one. Nothing in the suite could have revealed it: the test asserts ratios, not which block it read, and no other test reads tokens.css. It was found only because an unrelated change (the OS-default dark palette, which plain CSS forces to be a second copy of the same tokens) added an assertion that the two dark blocks are IDENTICAL -- and that comparison came back dark-versus-light. The defect surfaced as a diff in a test written for a different purpose. FIXED: block() now matches a selector only where it HEADS A RULE -- selector followed by optional whitespace and '{' -- and THROWS when no such rule exists, so a future selector rename fails loudly instead of silently grading something else. A second assertion checks the parsed block is non-empty before comparing, because {} equals {} and would pass vacuously. WHAT THE REPAIR REVEALED, and it is the reassuring half: with the parser fixed the dark cases ran against the real dark tokens for the first time and ALL PASS. The dark palette was always AA-compliant. Nothing was ever wrong with the design; the instrument was pointed at the wrong thing. SEVERITY is low on that basis -- no user was ever exposed to a failing contrast ratio -- but the control was absent rather than merely weak for the whole life of the file, and it was one of exactly two things standing between the dark theme and an accessibility regression. GENERALISES TO A RULE THIS PROJECT KEEPS RELEARNING: a check that locates its subject by substring can silently bind to prose ABOUT the subject. Same family as the seeding script whose body-grepping checks turned an expired token into three different fake data failures, and the DNS check that reported the resolver's address as the host's.

title: ALL SIX UAT E2E FAILURES CLASSIFIED (2026-08-11) — THREE HARNESS CAUSES PLUS ONE CONFIG MISMATCH. NO PRODUCT DEFECT, NO REGRESSION FROM DAYS 1-3, NO PRODUCTION EXPOSURE. Every one is the SAME underlying assumption in different clothing: the suite assumes a database seeded with EXACTLY its own fixtures and nothing else. CI rebuilds that database every run and is therefore blind to the entire class by construction, which is why 56 tests pass there and these do not — the difference was never the code. CAUSE 1, IDENTITY (p17b-voting AC-023/024, p17b-immutability x2 AC-022/AC-025) — FIXED AND VERIFIED: apiHelpers.ts:54 resolved the acting member with .find(m => m.role === acmpRole), a lookup keyed on a property that is NOT UNIQUE. Measured: E2E Chairman/Member/Secretary each hold TWO rows with distinct KeycloakUserId (DEF-029 orphans; a deleted Keycloak user strands its row forever and KeycloakUserId is uniquely indexed). The spec rostered one identity while the bearer carried the other, and RequireEligibleBallot's 'not eligible' throw surfaces as a 409 whose body is indistinguishable from 'already voted'. Replaced by meMember(), which resolves the caller's OWN row via POST /members/me -> publicId; three tests now pass. CAUSE 2, PAGINATION/VOLUME (ac043-reorder AC-043/FR-034, and dnd-and-failures x2 which were PASSING at 12:37 and failed by 15:00 with no code change): GetBacklog pages at 25; UAT holds 75 topics, 52 in Triage. New topics are priority 0 and the kanban sorts (Priority, CreatedAt, Key) ascending, so the newest sort LAST and fall past the fold — indexOf returned -1 for both fixtures, and dragHtml5 waited for a card never rendered. ⚠ THIS RATCHETS: every run creates topics, so each run makes the next MORE likely to fail. 'Six failures' was never a fixed number. Fixed by filtering the backlog to the run's own fixtures (search matches Title OR Key) before reading the column. CAUSE 3, ABSOLUTE COUNTS (p17b-meeting-vote AC-021): the spec asserts expect('.voter-row').toHaveCount(2) while the CallVoteDialog pre-selects every eligible voter. Measured on UAT: FOUR active voting-eligible members (chairman Seeded, E2E Chairman, E2E Member, member Seeded) plus two eligible-but-inactive. THE PRODUCT IS CORRECT — with four eligible members, rostering four is right; the test's fixed expectation of two is what only holds on a database containing exactly the e2e fixtures. NOT YET FIXED. CAUSE 4, ENVIRONMENT CONFIG (p17b-jobs AC-054/055) — NOT A HARNESS BUG AND NOT FIXABLE BY FILTERING: the spec polls 150 seconds for a Hangfire sweep, and its own header says the minutely cron is set 'in e2e'. Verified: e2e.yml:34 sets ACTION_REMINDERS_SWEEP_CRON='* * * * *' while docker-compose.cloud.yml:278 keeps the production default '0 6 * * *' — ONCE DAILY. The test is structurally incapable of passing against any deployed environment, and correctly so: nobody should give a deployed box a minutely production cron to satisfy a test. It should be SKIPPED with a stated reason when that override is absent, keeping its AC evidence on the CI run where the cron is real. HYPOTHESES KILLED BY MEASUREMENT: CPU throttling (balance ROSE 83->95, alarm OK); parallel-worker races (all reproduce at --workers=1); and my own claim that p17b-jobs shared the identity cause — it did not, the meMember fix landed and it still failed.

BOTH FAILURE BRANCHES WERE PROVEN BY FORCING THEM rather than by reading the code: adding view-realm produces 'grants view-realm beyond the proven minimum [manage-users]', and granting realm-admin adds 'ADR-0038 forbids it outright'. title: A SERVICE-ACCOUNT CLIENT IN realm-export.json WOULD NEVER HAVE EXISTED ON PROD OR UAT — FIXED 2026-08-12 (PR #237, main 122f41d) BY NOT BUILDING IT THAT WAY. Caught BEFORE writing the client, by reading reconcile.sh's own header: Keycloak imports the bundled realm export ONLY on first run and never re-imports an existing realm, so a client declared there reaches a fresh stack and silently does not appear on the two deployments that matter — while every health check stays green, because Keycloak itself is fine. That is the DEF-023 seam a third time (redirect URIs; CHANGE-004's `basic` scope; this). The SECRET settled it rather than merely reinforcing it: a confidential client's secret can only be made to match gen-secrets' file by being SET from that file, so the client cannot be fully expressed in a static export at all. FIX: reconcile.sh creates-or-updates the client on every boot in EVERY topology (prod is base+overlay, so the sidecar runs there too — checked, not assumed), re-asserts confidential + service-account-only, sets the secret FROM the mounted file, and reconciles the grant as an exact set. PROVEN, not assumed: CI's e2e log now carries "creating client 'acmp-admin-svc'", "confidential, service-account-only, secret set from the mounted file" and "realm-management grant is exactly: manage-users" on every run (DEF-051) — which is also the first empirical confirmation that kcadm's --uid flag works in practice rather than only in its help text.

title: THE WEBEX SECRETS ARE DELIVERED AS PLAIN COMPOSE `environment:` VARIABLES, WHICH IS THE ONE THING ADR-0032 SAYS NOT TO DO — AND THE FILE-BACKED SECRETS gen-secrets WRITES FOR THEM ARE MOUNTED BY NOTHING. Found 2026-08-12 while reading the Webex block as the PRECEDENT for wiring KeycloakAdmin's conditional secret, i.e. caught before copying it. gen-secrets.sh writes five files under deploy/secrets/ when WEBEX_ENABLED=true — Webex__BotToken, Webex__WebhookSecret, Webex__OAuthClientSecret, Webex__TokenEncryptionKey, Webex__OAuthSetupKey — and NO compose file declares any of them in a `secrets:` block or mounts them into any container. Verified across all three: docker-compose.yml, docker-compose.cloud.yml, docker-compose.prod.yml. Their secrets: blocks list only mssql_sa_password, minio_root_password, kc_db_password, kc_bootstrap_admin_password, keycloak_svc_password, acmp_svc_password, ConnectionStrings__Acmp, ConnectionStrings__AcmpMigrator and Minio__SecretKey. TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, and the second is the one that matters. (1) DEAD ARTIFACTS: five files containing real credentials are written to disk on every gen-secrets run and read by nobody — they exist only to be leaked. (2) THE ACTUAL DELIVERY PATH IS AN ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE: docker-compose.yml:202-210 pass Webex__BotToken, Webex__WebhookSecret, Webex__OAuthClientSecret and Webex__TokenEncryptionKey as `environment:` entries interpolated from .env. ADR-0032 chose file-backed secrets precisely to keep credentials OUT of compose environment blocks, because an environment value is readable by `docker inspect`, appears in the container's /proc/1/environ, and is captured by anything that dumps container config. So the app is reading its Webex credentials from the channel the ADR rejected while the channel the ADR chose sits unused beside it. EXPOSURE TODAY IS PROBABLY NIL BUT IS NOT VERIFIED: WEBEX_ENABLED=false in both .env.example (on-prem, line 34) and .env.cloud.example (UAT, OQ-062), so no real token should be interpolated — but the DEPLOYED env comes from SSM, not from the examples, and I did not read it. Confirm on prod/UAT before deciding severity. FIX (not in this slice): mount the five as compose secrets on api + worker and drop the environment entries, or — if the environment path is deliberate — delete the dead write_secret calls and record the deviation against ADR-0032 rather than leaving both halves half-done. NOTE FOR DW-024: this is why KeycloakAdmin__ClientSecret must NOT copy the Webex pattern; ADR-0038 says file-backed, so it gets a real compose secret entry mounted into api and keycloak-config.

title: A FAILED KEYCLOAK RECONCILE WAS SILENT IN CI — FIXED 2026-08-12 (PR #238, main 2a5ddde). An explicit e2e step now polls keycloak-config to `exited:0` and prints its log unconditionally. THE EXIT CODE IS THE CONVERGENCE ASSERTION, not a proxy: reconcile.sh reads its own post-conditions back (the acmp-web origin, and the service account's grant compared as an EXACT set) and returns non-zero when they did not take. ⚠ SCOPE CORRECTED TWICE, AND BOTH CORRECTIONS MATTER MORE THAN THE FIX. (1) I originally wrote 'nothing depends on keycloak-config in ANY compose file' and concluded nothing notices. The first clause is true and the conclusion was WRONG: aws/08-bootstrap-box.sh:271 already runs wait_oneshot over sqlserver-init, db-migrate AND keycloak-config, failing the deploy on a non-zero exit — written for exactly this silent-success family (DEF-017/018/020/024). I grepped compose and did not read the deploy script, so the CLOUD path had always been guarded. Severity high -> medium. (2) THE GUARD'S OWN FIRST RUN FAILED, AND FAILED IN THE WAY THE REPO HAD ALREADY DOCUMENTED: it reported `state=running:0` because I read the exit code while the container was still running — the bug PE-154 recorded in the local boot gate, spelled out in the comment on the very wait_oneshot helper I had just finished reading. Fixed by polling to `exited:*` with a deadline. THAT FAILURE ANSWERED THE QUESTION THIS DEFECT LEFT OPEN, which is why it was worth having: `docker compose up --wait` RETURNED WHILE THE ONE-SHOT WAS STILL MID-FLIGHT. So --wait offers no guarantee about a one-shot at all, and deploy/scripts/up.sh — which ends in exactly `up -d --wait` — CANNOT catch a failed reconcile on dev or ON-PREM PROD. That was recorded as unverified and is now MEASURED. EVIDENCE THIS PRODUCED, which is what the defect existed to make possible — the CI log now carries, on every run: "creating client 'acmp-admin-svc'", "'acmp-admin-svc' is confidential, service-account-only, secret set from the mounted file", "granted: manage-users", "realm-management grant is exactly: manage-users". That is the first proof in this repository that the ADR-0038 client is actually created, that reconcile.sh's kcadm `--uid` flag works in practice rather than merely appearing in the help text, and that the grant converges to the exact set OQ-070 proved. REMAINING (tracked, not fixed here): up.sh / the on-prem topology, where a silent reconcile failure reproduces DEF-023 exactly — now known to be unguarded rather than suspected. The heavier option, depends_on: keycloak-config { condition: service_completed_successfully } on api and worker, remains an operator availability decision because it converts a transient Keycloak hiccup into a refusal to start.

title: NO READ-SIDE ROLE GATE EXISTED: every content API was authenticated-only, so any principal - including the Guest that FR-159 creates - could read the ENTIRE governance record. FIXED 2026-08-12 (PR #241, main 5269cad), in the SAME merge as the writer that would have made it live. Verified by reading, not inferred: all 14 content groups in src/Acmp.Api/Endpoints/*.cs were `.MapGroup(...).RequireAuthorization()` with no policy, and every named policy in AuthorizationRegistration.Matrix is a WRITE capability - there was no 'read' row anywhere in the matrix. It was latent only because no Guest account had ever existed; FR-159's invite writer creates the first external principal, which is why the fix could not wait for a follow-up PR. WHAT SHIPPED: GuestSurfaceMiddleware, one scheme-agnostic DENY-BY-DEFAULT gate beside PrincipalRevalidationMiddleware. Deny-by-default rather than a policy per group deliberately (ADR-0040 decision 3): an opt-in policy protects only the endpoints somebody remembered to decorate, so every route added later would be open - the same shape as SC-005's JwtBearer hook silently exempting every future scheme. THE ALLOWLIST IS NOT A NEW JUDGEMENT: POST /api/members/me (without it a guest cannot complete a single sign-in, ADR-0004), /api/session (its own handler scopes the answer), /api/notifications (the bell renders in the shell for every user and the register is recipient-scoped), and GET-only /api/meetings (agenda is 'view' for Guest in the design's role matrix). The design demands the gate too - it draws a dedicated denial screen for a guest reaching a topic outside their session, with fixed bilingual copy. PROVEN BY FORCING THE REFUSAL, which matters more than usual here because the protected endpoints carry no authorization metadata of their own: 403 with reason `guest_scope` on 15 content paths, a guest may not WRITE to meetings even though it may read them, a committee member is unaffected, and a principal holding Guest AND a committee role is treated as an insider rather than locked out of their own committee. CONSEQUENCE RECORDED SEPARATELY: SC-007, because the gate contradicted AC-059's 'any authenticated role' for the Guest case - caught by an existing test, not by a gate.
